(1)

g(n)=∑d∣n​f(d)⟺f(n)=∑d∣n​μ(d)g(n/d).

Now
∑dk∣n​μ(d)
(3)

Let
cn​=∑1≤d≤n(d,n)=1​​e2πid/n.

For each degree and coefficient bound there are finitely many integer polynomials. Hence Z[x] is countable. Every nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots, and every algebraic number is a root of one of these polynomials. A countable union of finite sets is countable.

∑ℓ>j​anℓ​​<anj​​
(6)
for every j; this is possible because the tails of the convergent positive series tend to zero. Distinct binary sequences (εj​) then have distinct sums ∑j​εj​anj​​: at their first disagreement, the corresponding term exceeds the entire remaining tail. Thus these subsums form an uncountable set. The algebraic numbers are countable, so at least one subsum is transcendental. Set θnj​​=εj​ and all other θn​=0.

The unicity distance is the least ciphertext length for which the key is determined, or in the usual approximation the length at which the expected number of spurious keys falls to about zero. Assume equiprobable keys, a stationary plaintext source of information entropy rate HE​, and ciphertext symbols that are approximately uniform on A. The language redundancy per symbol is
D=log2​∣A∣−HE​.
(11)
The key equivocation is then approximated by
H(K∣C1​,ldots,Cn​)≃log2​∣K∣−nD.
(12)
Hence the classical closed-form estimate is
n0​≃log2​∣A∣−HE​log2​∣K∣​.
(13)

a OurBigBook.com
The homotopy lemma says that homotopic smooth maps between compact connected manifolds have the same mod-two degree, computed as the parity of the inverse image of a regular value. The homogeneity lemma says that any two points of a connected smooth manifold are related by a diffeomorphism isotopic to the identity.
Given regular values p,q of f, choose such a diffeomorphism h with h(p)=q. Then h∘f is homotopic to f, while (h∘f)−1(q)=f−1(p). The homotopy lemma proves that the two inverse-image counts have equal parity.
For smooth Brouwer, suppose a smooth self-map of a ball had no fixed point. Following the ray from f(x) through x to the boundary constructs a smooth retraction of the ball onto its sphere. Its restriction to the sphere is the identity, but it is also null-homotopic through the ball. The identity has odd mod-two degree and a constant map has even degree at a different regular value, contradicting the homotopy lemma. Thus a fixed point exists.

For a symmetric r-banded matrix, its subdiagonal entries can be eliminated by Givens rotations ordered along the band. Each rotation creates only the next local bulge; multiplication in reverse order chases that bulge out without creating entries beyond the original upper band.
